title: In the 1830s, Ketchup Was Sold as Medicine

scenes.text: In the 1830s, ketchup was sold as medicine.
Back then, most Americans thought tomatoes were poisonous. They looked too much like deadly nightshade berries.
Then in 1835, an Ohio doctor named John Cook Bennett announced that tomatoes cured indigestion and diarrhea. He told people to eat them as catsup.
By 1837, pharmacies were selling Extract of Tomato pills. Hundreds of thousands of people bought them.
Then doctors tested the pills. Many contained no tomato at all.
The craze died by 1850, but it taught America to eat tomatoes. Forty years later, Heinz was selling ketchup by the bottle. Fries without it. Could you?

description:
In the 1830s, ketchup was promoted and sold as medicine.
Ohio physician John Cook Bennett announced in 1835 that tomatoes cured indigestion and diarrhea and urged people to eat them as catsup; by 1837 Extract of Tomato pills were selling in pharmacies by the hundreds of thousands, until doctors found many contained no tomato at all. The craze faded by 1850, and Heinz added catsup to its product line in 1876.
Could you eat fries without ketchup?
